elicit

ih-LISS-it -- three syllables, stress on the second syllable, LISS. It sounds exactly like 'illicit' (meaning illegal), so watch the spelling. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To elicit is to draw a response, answer, or reaction out of a person.

The survey was designed to elicit honest answers rather than polite ones.

Example

The new counselor does not ask the boy what is wrong. She sets a jigsaw puzzle between them, works on it quietly for ten minutes, and by the time the border is finished he is telling her about the move.

The counselor elicited the story -- she drew it forth instead of demanding it. To elicit is to bring out a response, a reaction, or a piece of information that would not have come on its own.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

coax: To coax is to work on someone gently -- soft words, patience, small encouragements -- in the hope that they will give in. Coax names the effort and promises nothing about the result, while to elicit a response means the response actually came. You can coax all afternoon and elicit nothing.

obtain: To obtain is to succeed in getting anything at all -- a permit, a ticket, a signature. Elicit is narrower: what you get is a response, and you draw it out of a person, often with skill. You obtain a form from an office; you elicit an answer from a witness.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

suppress: hold something down so it cannot come out

withhold: deliberately keep something back

Where it sits · how deep a response it brings out — trigger → elicit → evoke

trigger vs. elicit: A trigger sets off only the ready-made surface reaction -- a startled jump, an automatic laugh -- while elicit reaches deeper, drawing out a response the person would not have offered on their own.

evoke vs. elicit: Evoke reaches deeper than elicit: a good question elicits an answer, but the smell of woodsmoke evokes an entire childhood. Elicit usually draws out information; evoke summons feelings and images.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — e-

prefix — e-: out (Latin ex-)

root — lic-

root — lic-: to entice, to lure (Latin lacere)

suffix — -it

suffix — -it: a Latin verb ending carried into English (Latin (-itus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin elicere combined e- ('out') with lacere ('to entice, to lure'), and -it is the Latin verb ending carried into English. To elicit is to lure something out into the open -- you do not seize the answer, you tempt it forward.

Use the root in a new word: delicious

Use the root in a new word: delicious: The smell from the bakery was so delicious that we changed our route just to walk past it.

Root Check

Word Choice

Elicit takes a response as its object: elicit a reaction, elicit information, elicit sympathy, elicit a confession. There is always someone or something you are drawing it out of. Beware the spelling trap -- illicit, with an i, is an adjective meaning illegal and has no connection at all.
